text: It [thought] is a mechanical thing and can solve only mechanical problems. But you want to use it to understand something living, and that is the problem.
note: Section 'Thinking Cannot Solve Your Problems' / topic index 'Thinking Is the Problem' on chandra.htm. First two sentences verbatim per Wikiquote/Quotepark; the closing clause is reconstructed from the snippet. Also attributed by one site to Mahesh Bhatt's A Taste of Death.

text: Food, clothing and shelter — these are the basic needs.
note: Opening of the passage under the 'Basic Needs' heading on chandra.htm; the full passage ends with a warning about self-deception. ru.citaty.net attributes the same lines to No Way Out (2002) ch. 4.

text: Tell them that there is nothing to understand.
note: Quoted in a reader review of the compilation; chandra.htm table of contents has a section 'There Is Nothing to Do'. Exact placement in Book Two not confirmed.

text: There is no moksha, no jivanmukti and no atman. And there is no such thing as self-realization.
note: From the chapter 'There Is No Moksha, No Jivanmukti and No Atman' — this is Book One (Stories of U.G. in India, from Chandrasekhar's notebooks), reproduced on the u-g-krishnamurti.blogspot mirror; not Book Two.

text: Why do you call it green?
note: Anecdote in Stopped in Our Tracks Part 1 (Book One) where U.G. questions a visitor who calls a tree green; wording from search snippet only.
Book One anecdote: when warned of burglaries U.G. said he was himself a thief; wording from search snippet.

text: My aim is to silence you.
note: chandra.htm passage on his approach says his aim is to silence [the audience]; exact phrasing not captured. Topic index also has 'Samadhi and Ultimate Samadhi'.

text: How I got into this state I will never be able to tell.
note: Reality Sandwich excerpt from the book (Mukunda Rao); followed by the statement that his autobiography comes to an end on 13 August 1967.

text: It is not a change in the structure of your thinking, but a change in the structure of the whole of your physical being.
note: Quoted in Mukunda Rao's Reality Sandwich introduction drawn from the 1967–71 conversations.

text: Whatever transformation I have undergone is within the structure of the human body and not in the mind at all.
note: Rao's introduction reports U.G. 'insists that whatever transformation he has undergone is within the structure of the human body and not in the mind at all'; converted to first person here.

text: I am not trying to sell anything here.
note: Snippet attributes this to the Paris (April 1967) conversation material; may instead come from The Mystique of Enlightenment. Verify.

text: The natural state is a pure and simple physical and physiological state of being, where it is not the self or the mind, but a different kind of intelligence that is in operation.
note: These are Mukunda Rao's editorial words describing U.G.'s state, not U.G.'s own; included for context only.

text: No one escapes the natural laws.
note: Ch. 1 'Stories of U.G. in Bangalore': U.G. dismisses Kelker's idea of detaching from pain. Book first printed Nov 1990 (Sowmya Publishers), reissued 2005 (Smriti Books).

text: It is the body that is immortal. It is living from moment to moment.
note: Wikiquote cites 'Quoted in The Sage and the Housewife (2005), Ch. 3'; the passage continues that people become rotten through culture. Quotepark attributes the same lines to No Way Out (2002) ch. 4.

text: I don't know what happiness is.
note: Ch. 4: asked by a visitor whether he is always happy, U.G. replies that he does not know what happiness is; wording from search snippet.

text: A person to whom Kundalini rises would dismiss the very concept of Kundalini.
note: Ch. 7 (U.G.'s November 1988 arrival in Bangalore); paraphrase from search snippet.

text: My teaching, if that is the word you want to use, has no copyright. You are free to reproduce, distribute, interpret, misinterpret, distort, garble, do what you like, even claim authorship, without my consent or the permission of anybody.
note: U.G.'s standard copyright disclaimer, printed in the front matter of his books and cited in Goodreads reviews of The Sage and the Housewife; not a line spoken in Kelker's narrative.
